newsitem.title: USA: Republicans, Democrats clash over funds probe.
newsitem.headline: Republicans, Democrats clash over funds probe.

text.p: Republicans and Democrats clashed Thursday through the halls of Congress over funding for launching investigations of campaign donations in the 1996 reeelection of President Bill Clinton.
Verbal battles took place in the House of Representatives and the Senate where separate investigations are planned into reported irregularities in campaign financing.
At issue was how much money the Republican-controlled Congress would approve for the probes and whether they would include the politically touchy issue of congressional campaign wrongdoing.
The campaign finance uproar has been a major embarrassment to the Clinton administration as reports emerge over questionable funds.
Besides pending congressional investigations, a 25-agent FBI task force is investigating illegalities, including whether the Chinese government gave money to U.S. campaigns.
On the Senate side, majority leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, announced a compromise in hopes of breaking a logjam to get the investigation started.
He said the Senate Rules Committee would consider the compromise and was expected to approve it later in the day for Senate action next week.
The compromise plan calls for spending $4.35 million -- less than sought by the top Senate Republican investigator but more than Democrats wanted.
A fight over funding has blocked the start of the Senate investigation by the Governmental Affairs Committee headed by Tennessee Republican Fred Thompson.

Thompson wanted $6.5 million. Democrats led by the party's senior committee member, John Glenn of Ohio, wanted $1.8 million. They also demanded the investigation cover congressional races as well as improprieties in the presidential election, a limit to the duration of hearings and a set date for discussing campaign finance reform.

In an effort for compromise, Lott proposed giving the committee $4.35 million, stipulating the investigation stop at the end of the year and expanding its scope to cover all allegedly "illegal" activities in both the presidential and the congressional races.
Senate minority leader Tom Daschle, a South Dakota Democrat, suggested his party would fight the plan, saying it has too much money and would limit investigations of Congress.
"My staff has advised they think it's a real problem (to cover only illegal offences) because you dont' know what is defined as legal and illegal at this stage," he said.
Lott suggested Democrats were out to block the probe.
"They said they wanted less money. This is less money," Lott told reporters. "They said they wanted some ending date. Everybody said you ought to include Congress. We're including it.
"How much do they want, or do they really just want to obstruct and block it?"

On the House side, the chief investigator, House Government Reform committee chairman Dan Burton, an Indiana Republican, asked the House Oversight Committee to approve $3.8 million to investigate "alleged fund-raising abuses of the Clinton Administration and the Democratic National Committee."

Representative Henry Waxman, a California Democrat who is senior minority member on Burton's committee, charged that Burton was running a "one-sided" investigation that would exclude congressional fund raising. He also said Democrats were not getting enough money out of Burton's committee request.
